docs.text: microlux is a Jax-based package that can calculate the binary lensing light curve and its derivatives both efficiently and accurately. We use the modified adaptive contour integratoin in VBBinaryLensing to maximize the performance. With the access to the gradient, we can use more advanced algorithms for microlensing modeling, such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) in numpyro.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Adaptive contour integration with error control to calculate the binary lens microlensing light curve with finite source effect.
  • Robust and accurate calculation: Widely test over the broad parameter space compared with VBBinaryLensing.
  • Fast speed: Fully compatible with JIT compilation to speed up calculation.
  • Accurate gradient: Automatic differentiation with specially designed error estimator to ensure the convergence of gradient.
  • Forward- and reverse-mode differentiation using implicit root derivatives on the final adaptive contour.
  • Aberth–Ehrlich method to find the roots of the polynomial and Liner sum assignment algorithm to match the images.
  • Application on the real event modeling.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Compute a binary-lens light curve with the example below. 

import jax.numpy as jnp
from microlux import binary_mag

# t0, u0, tE, rho, q, s, alpha in degrees
params = jnp.array([0.0, 0.1, 1.0, 0.01, 0.2, 0.9, 270.0])
times = jnp.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 1000)

mag = binary_mag(*params, times, tol=1e-3, retol=1e-3)

Detailed example usages are documented in the Quick Start Guide. Additional examples can be found in the test folder.

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: Calculate binary-lens magnification, then add annual parallax or orbital motion.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install microlux:

pip install microlux

Or install from source:

git clone https://github.com/CoastEgo/microlux.git
cd microlux
pip install -e .

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Binary Magnification
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from microlux import binary_mag

# t0, u0, tE, rho, q, s, alpha in degrees
params = jnp.array([0.0, 0.1, 1.0, 0.01, 0.2, 0.9, 270.0])
times = jnp.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 1000)

mag = binary_mag(*params, times, tol=1e-3, retol=1e-3)

docs.title: Example 2: Trajectory + Annual Parallax
docs.text:
import jax.numpy as jnp
from microlux.coordinates import Coordinates
from microlux.trajectory import TrajectoryParameters, get_trajectory_model
from microlux import extended_light_curve

# t0, u0, tE, rho, alpha in radians, s, q, pi_E_N, pi_E_E
params = jnp.array([
    2460000.0, 0.1, 100.0, 1e-3, jnp.deg2rad(120.0), 0.9, 1e-3, 0.1, 0.1,
])
params = TrajectoryParameters(*params)

times = jnp.linspace(params.t0 - 2.0 * params.tE, params.t0 + 2.0 * params.tE, 500)
coords = Coordinates(ra="17:59:02.3", dec="-29:04:15.2")
traj_model = get_trajectory_model(times=times, coords=coords, t0_par=params.t0)

trajectory, separation = traj_model.calculate_trajectory(params)
mag = extended_light_curve(trajectory, separation, params.q, params.rho)

docs.title: Example 3: Circular Orbital Motion, with Optional Parallax
docs.text:
The same trajectory model supports the effects independently:

Model t0_par orbital_motion Static None None Annual parallax Reference epoch None Circular orbit None "circular" Annual parallax + circular orbit Reference epoch "circular" 
import jax.numpy as jnp
from microlux import (
    Coordinates, TrajectoryParameters, get_trajectory_model, extended_light_curve,
)

# t0, u0, tE, rho, alpha in radians, s, q, pi_E_N, pi_E_E, gamma1, gamma2, gamma3
params = jnp.array([
    2460000.0, 0.1, 100.0, 0.01, 1.2, 1.3, 0.2,
    0.1, -0.1, 0.001, 0.002, 0.003,
])
params = TrajectoryParameters(*params)
times = jnp.linspace(params.t0 - 100.0, params.t0 + 100.0, 161)
model = get_trajectory_model(
    times,
    coords=Coordinates(ra="17:59:02.3", dec="-29:04:15.2"),
    t0_par=2459983.0,
    orbital_motion="circular",
    photo_center=True,
)
trajectory, separation = model.calculate_trajectory(params)
mag = extended_light_curve(trajectory, separation, params.q, params.rho)

trajectory and separation are arrays of shape (N,), giving the source position and lens separation at each observation. Pass both to extended_light_curve; without orbital motion, separation is constant.

docs.title: Fitting
docs.text: Fit source and blend fluxes for several photometric data sets and compute a Fisher matrix from the resulting residuals.

docs.title: microlux.fit_grouped_fluxes(magnification: jax.Array, flux: jax.Array, flux_err: jax.Array, group_ids: jax.Array, *, n_groups: int) -> GroupedFluxFit
docs.text:
Fit source and blend fluxes for each group with JAX.

Parameters:

  • magnification (Array) –

    Finite magnifications of shape (N,).

  • flux (Array) –

    Finite observed fluxes of shape (N,).

  • flux_err (Array) –

    Positive uncertainties of shape (N,). Use infinity for zero-weight padding with finite flux and magnification.

  • group_ids (Array) –

    Integer labels of shape (N,), contiguous from zero to n_groups - 1. Observations may be interleaved.

  • n_groups (int) –

    Number of groups, fixed when tracing a JIT function.

Returns:

  • result ( GroupedFluxFit ) –

    Weighted least-squares solution of flux = source_flux[group_ids] * magnification + blend_flux[group_ids]. Differentiation includes the dependence of the fitted fluxes on the supplied magnifications.

Notes

Accepts NumPy or JAX arrays and supports JIT and automatic differentiation. Each group needs a full-rank weighted source/blend design. Validate data values and handle degenerate fits in the caller. Only shapes and label dtype are checked here.

docs.title: microlux.binary_mag(t_0, u_0, t_E, rho, q, s, alpha_deg, times: jnp.ndarray, tol=0.01, retol=0.001, default_strategy: Tuple[int] = (30, 30, 60, 120, 240), analytic: bool = True, return_info: bool = False, limb_darkening_coeff: float | None = None)
docs.text:
Compute the light curve of a binary lens system with finite source effects. This function will dynamically choose full contour integration or point source approximation based on the point-source validity checks.

Note

The coordinate system is consistent with the MulensModel(Center of mass).

Warning

Currently, to deal with limb-darkening effect, we only use 10 annuli which are uniformly distributed in terms of the area, which is not in an adaptive scheme. So the tolerance of the limb darkening effect is not guaranteed.

Parameters:

  • t_0 –

    The time of closest approach to the center of mass.

  • u_0 –

    The impact parameter of the source trajectory.

  • t_E –

    The Einstein crossing time.

  • rho –

    The source radius normalized to the Einstein radius.

  • q –

    The mass ratio of the secondary lens to the primary lens.

  • s –

    The projected separation of the binary lens system normalized to the Einstein radius.

  • alpha_deg –

    The angle between the source trajectory and the binary axis in degrees.

  • times (ndarray) –

    The times at which to compute the model.

  • tol –

    The tolerance for the adaptive contour integration. Defaults to 1e-2.

  • retol –

    The relative tolerance for the adaptive contour integration. Defaults to 0.001.

  • default_strategy (Tuple[int], default: (30, 30, 60, 120, 240) ) –

    The default strategy for the contour integration. Defaults to (30, 30, 60, 120, 240). more details can be found in the microlux.contour_integral.

  • analytic (bool, default: True ) –

    Use implicit root derivatives on the final contour mesh to support forward- and reverse-mode differentiation. Defaults to True. If False, differentiate through the adaptive iterations in forward mode.

  • return_info (bool, default: False ) –

    Whether to return additional information about the computation. Defaults to False. when set to True, the function will return a tuple containing (magnification, info), where info is a tuple containing additional information about the computation used for debugging.

  • limb_darkening_coeff (float | None, default: None ) –

    The limb darkening coefficient for the source star. Defaults to None for a uniformly bright source. Currently only supports linear limb darkening.

Returns:

  • magnification –

    The magnification of the source at the given times.

  • info –

    Additional information about the computation used for debugging if return_info is True. The structure is (trajectory_l, rho, s, q, roots_state, error_state), with an epoch axis on the arrays. trajectory_l uses the low-mass lens coordinate system. Point-source epochs contain placeholder contour states; use the returned magnification array for the light curve. See microlux.utils.Iterative_State and microlux.utils.Error_State for state fields.

  • return_num (bool, default: False ) –

  • cond –

A tuple (magnification, cond), or (magnification, cond, image_count) if return_num=True.

Compute the light curve of a binary lens system with finite source effects.

Note

The trajectory parameter should be in the center-of-mass coordinate system (consistent with MulensModel). The function internally transforms to low-mass coordinates for the calculation.

Parameters:

For the definition of the other parameters, please see microlux.binary_mag.

docs.title: microlux.contour_integral(trajectory_l, tol, retol, rho, s, q, default_strategy=(60, 80, 150), analytic=True) -> Tuple[jnp.ndarray, Tuple]
docs.text:
Perform adaptive contour integration with pre-define shaped array. This function is used to reduce the memory usage and improve the performance of the contour integration. The reason is that the optimal fixed array length is hard to determine before the code runs which the basic requirement for JIT compilation. If the array length is too small, the adaptive contour integration will stop early and the error will be larger than the tolerance. If the array length is too large, it will cause the waste of memory and time. This waste is linear with the array length. So we use this pre-define shaped array to solve this problem.

Parameters:

  • trajectory_l –

    Source position in the low-mass lens coordinate system. Convert center-of-mass coordinates with to_lowmass before calling this function.

  • default_strategy –

    The default strategy for the contour integration. The array length will be added gradually according to this strategy. For example, if the default_strategy is (60, 80, 150), the array length in each layer will be 60, 140, 290, respectively.

  • analytic –

    Use implicit root derivatives on the final sampling mesh to support forward- and reverse-mode differentiation. Defaults to True. If False, differentiate through the adaptive iterations in forward mode.

For other parameters: please see at microlux.binary_mag

Returns:

  • result ( Tuple[ndarray, Tuple] ) –

    A tuple (magnification, info), where info = (trajectory_l, rho, s, q, roots_state, error_state).

If the contour capacity is exhausted, error_state.exceed_flag is True and the requested tolerance may be unmet. Increase default_strategy and recompute to allow further refinement.

Returns:

docs.title: Trajectory
docs.text: Trajectory utilities for building source tracks in the center-of-mass frame, with independently optional annual parallax and circular orbital motion.

docs.title: microlux.trajectory.TrajectoryParameters
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

A NamedTuple containing microlensing trajectory parameters.

Orbital rates follow VBMicrolensing and are defined at the center-of-mass t0. They are ignored unless orbital motion is enabled.

Attributes:

  • t0 (ndarray) –

    Time of closest approach, in days.

  • u0 (ndarray) –

    Impact parameter at t0.

  • tE (ndarray) –

    Einstein timescale in days.

  • rho (ndarray) –

    Source radius in units of Einstein radius.

  • alpha_rad (ndarray) –

    Trajectory angle in radians.

  • s (ndarray) –

    Projected lens separation in Einstein-radius units.

  • q (ndarray) –

    Lens mass ratio.

  • pi_E_N (ndarray) –

    North component of microlensing parallax vector. Only used when parallax is enabled.

  • pi_E_E (ndarray) –

    East component of microlensing parallax vector. Only used when parallax is enabled.

  • gamma1 (ndarray) –

    Fractional projected-separation rate (ds/dt)/s, in day^-1.

  • gamma2 (ndarray) –

    Angular rate in rad day^-1, with the sign following the VBM trajectory convention.

  • gamma3 (ndarray) –

    Fractional line-of-sight separation rate (ds_z/dt)/s, in day^-1.

docs.title: microlux.trajectory.TrajectoryModel
docs.text:
Bases: NamedTuple

A trajectory model with independent parallax and circular-orbit effects.

Attributes:

  • times (ndarray) –

    Observation times in Julian Date.

  • delta_s (ndarray | None) –

    Observer displacement in AU projected on the sky plane in (North, East), shape (N, 2). If None, parallax correction is disabled.

  • photo_center (bool) –

    Whether input parameters use the magnification center for s > 1. Output trajectories always use the center of mass.

  • orbital_motion (str | None) –

    None or "circular". Independent of delta_s.

docs.title: calculate_trajectory(params: TrajectoryParameters | np.ndarray | jnp.ndarray) -> tuple[jnp.ndarray, jnp.ndarray]
docs.text:
Return (source trajectory, lens separation), each with shape (N,).

The trajectory uses center-of-mass coordinates in the instantaneous binary-axis frame. Without orbital motion, separation is constant.

Parameters may be a TrajectoryParameters instance or a 1D array: [t0, u0, tE, rho, alpha_rad, s, q], followed by [pi_E_N, pi_E_E] when parallax is enabled. Circular motion appends [gamma1, gamma2, gamma3] (10/12 entries without/with parallax).

The returned trajectory is complex and separation is real; pass both to extended_light_curve. To plot only the source, unpack trajectory, _.

Reference frame

With photo_center=False, the orbital reference epoch is params.t0. With photo_center=True and s > 1, input parameters refer to the magnification center and are converted to the center of mass:

shift = q / (1 + q) * (s - 1 / s)
t0_com = t0 + tE * shift * cos(alpha_rad)
u0_com = u0 + shift * sin(alpha_rad)

The shift uses the reference separation s and stays fixed along the trajectory; it is not recomputed from s(t). For s <= 1 it is zero. The reference s, alpha_rad, and orbital rates refer to t0_com. The parallax reference epoch t0_par is independent of this epoch.

Circular orbit

Away from the numerical boundary handling below, the circular constraint fixes the line-of-sight separation s_z/s = -gamma1/gamma3 at the reference epoch. The projected separation can therefore vary even though the three-dimensional orbit is circular.

Following VBMicrolensing, hypot(gamma1, gamma3) <= 1e-8 selects a face-on orbit with constant separation and angular rate gamma2. All-zero rates recover the static/parallax model. Otherwise abs(gamma3) is floored at 1e-8 day^-1, preserving its sign and taking zero as positive. Opposite signs give the same projected orbit. This numerical convention does not uniquely continue the physical orbit through the degenerate parameters.

Fitting

Start a full orbital fit near static with (gamma1, gamma2, gamma3) = (0, 0, 1e-6), rather than all zeros. RTModel uses a gamma3 lower bound of 1e-7 day^-1 in its fitter; configure such a bound in your optimizer or sampler, since this forward model does not impose it. Derivatives in the floored region or across the branch boundary follow the numerical guard; avoid those regions for inference and Fisher calculations.

docs.title: microlux.trajectory.get_trajectory_model(times: np.ndarray, coords: Coordinates | None = None, t0_par: float | None = None, photo_center: bool = False, *, orbital_motion: str | None = None) -> TrajectoryModel
docs.text:
Build a trajectory model with optional annual parallax and circular orbit.

Parameters:

  • times (ndarray) –

    Observation epochs in full JD or reduced JD (JD - 2450000).

  • coords (Coordinates | None, default: None ) –

    Source sky coordinates; required only for annual parallax.

  • t0_par (float | None, default: None ) –

    Parallax reference epoch. If None, parallax is disabled.

  • photo_center (bool, default: False ) –

    Whether input parameters use the magnification center for s > 1; output is always in the center-of-mass frame.

  • orbital_motion (str | None, default: None ) –

    None or "circular", independently of parallax.

Returns:

  • trajectory_model ( TrajectoryModel ) –

    Trajectory model instance.

Notes
  • Use the same full or reduced JD convention for times, t0, and t0_par.
  • Annual ephemerides are precomputed here, outside JAX differentiation. The returned model stores the observer displacement in delta_s, in AU projected onto North/East. This factory computes annual parallax only.
  • Named TrajectoryParameters work with every combination of effects. See TrajectoryModel.calculate_trajectory for array layouts, reference frames, and orbital boundary handling.

docs.title: Modeling KB-19-0371 with microlux
docs.text:
Fit KB-19-0371 using SciPy and automatic differentiation, then sample with Fisher-reparameterized HMC and compare with an optional emcee chain.

import os
import sys
from multiprocessing.pool import ThreadPool
from pathlib import Path


N_PMAP = 10
HMC_NUM_CHAINS = 1
RUN_HMC = True
HMC_NUM_WARMUP = 500
HMC_NUM_SAMPLES = 1000
TARGET_ACCEPT = 0.8
RUN_EMCEE = False
EMCEE_NWALKERS = 20
EMCEE_NUM_WARMUP = 500
EMCEE_NUM_SAMPLES = 1000
BOUNDARY_STEEPNESS = 100.0
PENALTY_STRENGTH = 1000.0

os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"] = (
    f"--xla_force_host_platform_device_count={N_PMAP * HMC_NUM_CHAINS}"
)
if "__file__" in globals():
    EXAMPLE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
elif Path("event_utils.py").exists():
    EXAMPLE_DIR = Path.cwd()
else:
    EXAMPLE_DIR = Path.cwd() / "example"
sys.path.insert(0, str(EXAMPLE_DIR))
FIGURE_DIR = EXAMPLE_DIR / "figures"
FIGURE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

import corner

docs.title: Photometric data preparation
docs.text:
Filter the photometry and rescale the reported uncertainties. Alignment to the OGLE flux system is used only for plotting.

if jax.local_device_count() < N_PMAP * HMC_NUM_CHAINS:
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"Restart the Python kernel so XLA_FLAGS can set {N_PMAP * HMC_NUM_CHAINS} CPU devices."
    )

data = pd.read_csv(EXAMPLE_DIR / "data" / "KB_19_0371.csv")

cond = (data["e_mag"] < 0.4) & (data["HJD"] > 8500)
data = data[cond].copy()

error_frac = {
    "OGLE": 1.59,
    "KMTC01": 1.41,
    "KMTC41": 1.38,
    "KMTA01": 1.35,
    "KMTA41": 1.57,

}
data["e_mag"] = np.hypot(0.003, data["e_mag"] * data["Tel"].map(error_frac))

docs.title: Close binary-lens solution
docs.text:
Start from the close solution and fit the source and blend fluxes for each data set. Use the fitted OGLE fluxes to align the light-curve plot.

parms_close = {
    "t0": 8592.388619,
    "u0": 0.140631,
    "tE": 6.655161,
    "logrho": -2.231148,
    "alpha": 271.695690,
    "logs": -0.079158,
    "logq": -1.141006,
}
# parms_wide = {'t0': 8592.391925, 'u0': 0.144696, 'tE': 6.640740, 'logrho': -2.187052, 'alpha': 271.325666, 'logs': 0.188680, 'logq': -0.957499}

observation_times = data["HJD"].values
optimization_start = np.array([parms_close[name] for name in PARAMETER_NAMES])
group_ids, telescope_names = pd.factorize(data["Tel"], sort=True)
fit_times = jnp.asarray(observation_times)
fit_flux, fit_error = mag_to_flux(data["mag"].values, data["e_mag"].values)
fit_flux, fit_error = jnp.asarray(fit_flux), jnp.asarray(fit_error)
group_ids = jnp.asarray(group_ids)


@jax.jit
def grouped_flux_fit(params):
    magnification = light_curve_Jax(params, fit_times)
    return fit_grouped_fluxes(
        magnification,
        fit_flux,
        fit_error,
        group_ids,
        n_groups=len(telescope_names),
    )


initial_flux_fit = grouped_flux_fit(jnp.asarray(optimization_start))
fs = np.asarray(initial_flux_fit.source_flux)
fb = np.asarray(initial_flux_fit.blend_flux)
ogle_group = telescope_names.get_loc("OGLE")
data["mag_aligned"], data["e_mag_aligned"] = align_function(
    data["mag"].values,
    data["e_mag"].values,
    fs[group_ids],
    fb[group_ids],
    fs[ogle_group],
    fb[ogle_group],
)

plot_times = np.linspace(8500, 8800, 2000)
mag_close = light_curve_VBBL(plot_times, parms_close)
flux_close = mag_close * fs[ogle_group] + fb[ogle_group]
mag_close = flux_to_mag(flux_close)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
all_tel = data["Tel"].unique()
for i in all_tel:
    tel_data = data[data["Tel"] == i]
    ax.errorbar(
        tel_data["HJD"],
        tel_data["mag_aligned"],
        yerr=tel_data["e_mag_aligned"],
        fmt="o",
        label=i,
    )
ax.plot(plot_times, mag_close, label="Close solution")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
ax.set_xlim(8580, 8600)
ax.set_xlabel("HJD")
ax.set_ylabel("Magnitude")
ax.invert_yaxis()

ax_traj = fig.add_axes([0.2, 0.6, 0.25, 0.25])
tau = (plot_times - parms_close["t0"]) / parms_close["tE"]
alpha = parms_close["alpha"] / 180 * np.pi
y1 = -parms_close["u0"] * np.sin(alpha) + tau * np.cos(alpha)
y2 = parms_close["u0"] * np.cos(alpha) + tau * np.sin(alpha)
ax_traj.plot(y1, y2, c="black")
ax_traj.set_aspect("equal")
ax_traj.set_xlim(-1.0, 1.0)
ax_traj.set_ylim(-1.0, 1.0)
caustics_instance = CausticsBinary(
    s=10 ** parms_close["logs"], q=10 ** parms_close["logq"]
)
caustics_x, caustics_y = caustics_instance.get_caustics()
ax_traj.scatter(caustics_x, caustics_y, c="r", s=1)

save_figure(fig, "KB0371_close_solution.png")
display(fig)

docs.title: Gradient optimization with SciPy and JAX
docs.text:
Optimize the seven lens parameters with scipy.optimize.least_squares, using the residual Jacobian supplied by JAX automatic differentiation.

parameter_bounds = np.array(
    [
        [optimization_start[0] - 50.0, optimization_start[0] + 50.0],
        [-2.0, 2.0],
        [0.1, 200.0],
        [-4.0, -2.0],
        [0.0, 360.0],
        [-1.5, 1.5],
        [-4.0, 3.0],
    ]
)


def profiled_residuals(params):
    return grouped_flux_fit(params).residuals


residual_jacobian = jax.jacfwd(profiled_residuals)

optimization = least_squares(
    profiled_residuals,
    optimization_start,
    jac=residual_jacobian,
    bounds=parameter_bounds.T,
    x_scale="jac",
    max_nfev=100,
    verbose=1,
)
optimized_params = optimization.x
optimized_flux_fit = grouped_flux_fit(jnp.asarray(optimized_params))
print("Optimizer:", optimization.message)
print("Initial chi2:", float(jnp.sum(initial_flux_fit.chi2_by_group)))
print("Optimized chi2:", float(jnp.sum(optimized_flux_fit.chi2_by_group)))
print(
    "Degrees of freedom:",
    len(fit_times) - len(optimization_start) - 2 * len(telescope_names),
)
display(
    pd.DataFrame(
        {"initial": optimization_start, "optimized": optimized_params},
        index=PARAMETER_NAMES,
    )
)
display(
    pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "source_flux": np.asarray(optimized_flux_fit.source_flux),
            "blend_flux": np.asarray(optimized_flux_fit.blend_flux),
            "chi2": np.asarray(optimized_flux_fit.chi2_by_group),
        },
        index=telescope_names,
    )
)

docs.title: Local Fisher approximation
docs.text:
HMC can become inefficient when the posterior is strongly correlated or has very different scales along different directions. Following the discussion in the NumPyro tutorial Bad posterior geometry and how to deal with it, we change the coordinate system before running HMC.

For Gaussian observational errors, we approximate the local Fisher matrix from the Jacobian of the normalized residuals at optimized_params:

\[ r_i(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{f_i - f_{\mathrm{model},i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\sigma_i}, \qquad J_{ij} = \frac{\partial r_i}{\partial \theta_j}, \] \[ F = J^\mathsf{T} J, \qquad C \approx F^{-1}. \]

profiled_residuals refits the source and blend fluxes at each lens parameter vector, so their parameter dependence is included in the Jacobian. Here, \(C\) approximates the local covariance of the seven lens parameters and supplies the scales and correlations for HMC below.

fisher_matrix = fisher_information(profiled_residuals, jnp.asarray(optimized_params))
fisher_cov = jnp.linalg.inv(fisher_matrix)
display(
    pd.Series(
        np.sqrt(np.diag(np.asarray(fisher_cov))),
        index=PARAMETER_NAMES,
        name="Local parameter uncertainty",
    )
)

docs.title: Fisher reparameterization for HMC
docs.text:
Set \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\) to optimized_params and compute the lower triangular Cholesky factor \(L\) of fisher_cov. NUTS samples the latent coordinates \(\boldsymbol{z}\) and maps them to the lens parameters:

\[ C = L L^\mathsf{T}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_0 + L \boldsymbol{z}. \]

Under the local Gaussian approximation, the covariance of these new coordinates is

\[ \operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{z}) \approx L^{-1} C L^{-\mathsf{T}} = I. \]

This reduces scale differences and correlations near the fitted solution. We compute \(L\) once and keep it fixed during sampling; dense_mass=True lets NumPyro adapt the remaining correlations during warmup.

In the model, param_base stores \(\boldsymbol{z}\) and param records \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). Initializing param_base at zero starts the chain at optimized_params. Every likelihood evaluation uses the full light curve at the transformed parameters.

dist.ImproperUniform keeps the latent prior flat. Since \(L\) is fixed, the change-of-variables Jacobian determinant is constant: this reparameterization does not add a Gaussian prior. The boundary penalties are still evaluated in the original lens coordinates.

Pad only the times for parallel evaluation, then trim the predictions before evaluating the likelihood and chi2.

padding = (-fit_times.shape[0]) % N_PMAP
time_chunks = jnp.pad(fit_times, (0, padding), mode="edge").reshape(-1, N_PMAP).T
parallel_light_curve = jax.pmap(light_curve_Jax, in_axes=(None, 0))

param_lowers = jnp.array(parameter_bounds[:, 0])
param_uppers = jnp.array(parameter_bounds[:, 1])

initial_param = jnp.asarray(optimized_params)
if bool(jnp.any(initial_param <= param_lowers)) or bool(
    jnp.any(initial_param >= param_uppers)
):
    raise ValueError("Initial parameters must be strictly inside soft boundaries.")

cholesky_transform = jnp.linalg.cholesky(fisher_cov)

docs.title: HMC model
docs.text:
Fit the source and blend fluxes at each likelihood evaluation. Clip lens parameters to the numerical domain and apply a soft boundary penalty.

def model_HMC_reparameterized(
    data,
    group_ids,
    n_groups,
    init_val,
    transform_matrix,
    param_lowers,
    param_uppers,
    boundary_steepness,
    penalty_strength,
):
    time_chunks, flux, ferr = data
    param_base = numpyro.sample(
        "param_base",
        dist.ImproperUniform(constraints.real, (), event_shape=(len(init_val),)),
    )
    parmsample = jnp.dot(transform_matrix, param_base) + jnp.asarray(init_val)
    numpyro.deterministic("param", parmsample)

    lower_penalty = jnp.sum(softplus(boundary_steepness * (param_lowers - parmsample)))
    upper_penalty = jnp.sum(softplus(boundary_steepness * (parmsample - param_uppers)))
    penalty = lower_penalty + upper_penalty
    safe_params = jnp.clip(parmsample, param_lowers + 1e-5, param_uppers - 1e-5)

    mag_mod = parallel_light_curve(safe_params, time_chunks).T.reshape(-1)
    mag_mod = mag_mod[: flux.shape[0]]
    flux_fit = fit_grouped_fluxes(mag_mod, flux, ferr, group_ids, n_groups=n_groups)
    numpyro.sample("obs", dist.Normal(flux_fit.model_flux, ferr), obs=flux)
    numpyro.factor("boundary_penalty", -penalty_strength * penalty)
    chi2 = jnp.sum(flux_fit.chi2_by_group)
    numpyro.deterministic("source_flux", flux_fit.source_flux)
    numpyro.deterministic("blend_flux", flux_fit.blend_flux)
    numpyro.deterministic("chi2", chi2)
    numpyro.deterministic("penalty", penalty)

if RUN_HMC:
    init_strategy = numpyro.infer.init_to_value(
        values={"param_base": jnp.zeros(len(initial_param))}
    )
    nuts_kernel = NUTS(
        model_HMC_reparameterized,
        step_size=1.0 / 5.0,
        target_accept_prob=TARGET_ACCEPT,
        init_strategy=init_strategy,
        forward_mode_differentiation=True,
        dense_mass=True,
        adapt_mass_matrix=True,
    )
    mcmc = MCMC(
        nuts_kernel,
        num_warmup=HMC_NUM_WARMUP,
        num_samples=HMC_NUM_SAMPLES,
        num_chains=HMC_NUM_CHAINS,
        progress_bar=True,
    )

    mcmc.run(
        jax.random.PRNGKey(0),
        data=[time_chunks, fit_flux, fit_error],
        group_ids=group_ids,
        n_groups=len(telescope_names),
        init_val=initial_param,
        transform_matrix=cholesky_transform,
        param_lowers=param_lowers,
        param_uppers=param_uppers,
        boundary_steepness=BOUNDARY_STEEPNESS,
        penalty_strength=PENALTY_STRENGTH,
    )
    mcmc.print_summary(exclude_deterministic=False)
else:
    print("Skipping HMC; set RUN_HMC = True to run it.")

docs.title: emcee reference chain
docs.text:
Start emcee from optimized_params, using VBM with the same grouped fit and boundary penalties as HMC.

def log_probability(params):
    lower, upper = parameter_bounds.T
    penalty = np.sum(np.logaddexp(0.0, BOUNDARY_STEEPNESS * (lower - params)))
    penalty += np.sum(np.logaddexp(0.0, BOUNDARY_STEEPNESS * (params - upper)))
    safe_params = np.clip(params, lower + 1e-5, upper - 1e-5)
    magnification = light_curve_VBBL(
        observation_times, dict(zip(PARAMETER_NAMES, safe_params))
    )
    flux_fit = fit_grouped_fluxes(
        magnification,
        fit_flux,
        fit_error,
        group_ids,
        n_groups=len(telescope_names),
    )
    return -0.5 * float(jnp.sum(flux_fit.chi2_by_group)) - PENALTY_STRENGTH * penalty

n_dim = len(optimized_params)
step_size = 0.001 * np.ones_like(optimized_params)
if RUN_EMCEE:
    pos = [
        optimized_params + step_size * np.random.randn(n_dim)
        for i in range(EMCEE_NWALKERS)
    ]
    with ThreadPool(EMCEE_NWALKERS) as pool:
        sampler = emcee.EnsembleSampler(
            EMCEE_NWALKERS,
            n_dim,
            log_probability,
            pool=pool,
        )
        pos, _, _ = sampler.run_mcmc(pos, EMCEE_NUM_WARMUP, progress=True)
        sampler.reset()
        sampler.run_mcmc(pos, EMCEE_NUM_SAMPLES, progress=True)
else:
    print("Skipping emcee; set RUN_EMCEE = True to run it.")

if RUN_EMCEE:
    emcee_samples = sampler.get_chain()
    print_summary(np.transpose(emcee_samples, (1, 0, 2)))

if RUN_EMCEE:
    emcee_chain = sampler.get_chain(flat=True)
    fig = corner.corner(
        emcee_chain,
        labels=PARAMETER_NAMES,
        quantiles=[0.16, 0.5, 0.84],
        show_titles=True,
        truths=np.median(emcee_chain, axis=0),
    )
    save_figure(fig, "KB0371_emcee_corner.png")
    plt.show()

Compare the local Fisher approximation (red) with the emcee posterior (blue).

if RUN_EMCEE:
    fig, axes = plot_covariance(
        optimized_params, PARAMETER_NAMES, np.asarray(fisher_cov), emcee_chain
    )
    save_figure(fig, "KB0371_fisher_covariance.png")
    plt.show()
